I am noticing price doesn't always bounce so nicely from these levels - usually there is a reaction, but some are better than others. There must be a reason for this.

Going back to the USD-CHF example I posted above (post #834): This reaction was perfect - an incredible R:R. What was it about this setup that made the bounce so strong? There were two main engulfs - both had targets. Both engulfs had hit their targets before price came back down to the level in question... But it still bounced strongly and revisited the previous engulf's target. It seems odd that price would react that way considering the engulf already hit its target.

What am I not seeing?

The difference between en engulf and a fakeout (based on my understanding) depends on the location of the engulf/fakeout. A engulf happens in to an area of no significance (no important OF). A fakeout has a specific purpose - to get liquidity. So fakeouts occur in to areas with substantial OF.

The areas of a chart that have the most OF or liquidity is FTR's/FL's.

Flag limits are also FTR's - and these areas of price structure contain important decision points. These Fl's/FTR's also represent the extreme levels of a particular flag and mark the upper/lower boundaries of price action zones (PAZ).

Maybe the key to finding the best areas for a reaction/bounce is focusing more on what the initial fakeout is reacting to (look further left).

Are all HH/LL in a QM a fakeout? Is it possible to have a QM form without a fakeout?

Is a Diamond made up of two fakeouts? One of the HH/LL portion of the QM and another for the diamond formation (which fakeouts the initial fakeout).

More diagrams - can both of these be true? If price breaks in to a PAZ it is supposed to be en engulf - but what if price breaks in to a PAZ while forming a QM? Is the HH portion of the QM a fakeout even through it happened in an area without important OF?

Thanks Edge - I guess my confusion is related to the fractal analysis that must occur in every decision EG vs. FO - For example, if price breaks in to a HTF PAZ (pretty easy to identify times where this happens), we assume it has engulfed.I am always curious why price stops where it does after the engulf and before the RT. On a lower time frame, price may have seemed to EG in to the HTF PAZ, but it engulfs in to a lower time frame FL/FTR. How do we read that? Fakeouts have a specific purpose - to find liquidity in the form of OF. EG's occur in areas of insignificance (with regard to OF).

Do you have any ideas why USD-CHF bounced so nicely at that level compared to other times when price doesn't bounce so far? I have been sitting here trying to figure out why some of these entrees are more powerful than others. I think the answer may lie in engulfs vs fakeouts and OF. Can't seem to figure it out...

Also, if fakeouts occur in to areas of liquidity, we have to assume every HH or LL of a QM is a fakeout - not an engulf. Right? Engulfs are directional, and the HH (of a bearish QM) certainly doesn't represent direction of price....price is moving the opposite direction of the HH...price wants the target of the engulf that happens before the fakeout. The whole point of the HH is to trap breakout traders and trigger stops. I am confusing myself
